lessons.title: How Exchanges Publish Data — Snapshots vs Tick-by-Tick Feeds

children.text: Two firms can subscribe to NSE's market data and see two different versions of the same order book, not because either one is wrong, but because they are not actually receiving the same feed. What an exchange calls its market data is really at least two different products, built for two different audiences.
Two Ways to Tell the Market What Happened

markDefs.definition: A market data feed that periodically broadcasts the current state of the order book at fixed intervals, rather than announcing every individual change as it happens.

children.text: periodically broadcasts the current state of the order book, for example the best few price levels, once every second or even less often, rather than announcing each individual change as it happens. It is compact, easy to consume, and good enough for a dashboard or a retail charting app. It is nowhere near good enough for a strategy that needs to know the exact order in which two events occurred. That is what the tick-by-tick (TBT) data feed, introduced in the previous chapter, exists to solve: it announces every single order book event individually, in the exact sequence the matching engine processed them.

cells: Periodic order book state, e.g. once a second
Dashboards, retail apps, anything that doesn't need exact event order
Every individual order book event, in matching engine sequence
HFT strategies, order book reconstruction, anything latency-sensitive

children.text: Why Multicast, and Why Sequence Numbers Matter

markDefs.definition: A network transmission method where a single stream of data is broadcast once and can be received by any number of listening subscribers simultaneously, rather than the sender maintaining a separate connection per recipient.

children.text: Exchanges do not send market data to each subscriber over its own dedicated connection. They use

: a single stream broadcast once onto the network, which every subscriber's server can listen to simultaneously, the same way a radio station transmits once and everyone with a receiver hears it. This scales to thousands of colocated servers without the exchange having to manage thousands of individual connections.

markDefs.definition: A number attached to each message in a market data feed, increasing by one with every message, that lets a subscriber detect a dropped packet by noticing a gap in the sequence.

children.text: Multicast, however, does not guarantee delivery. A packet can be dropped, and the sender has no way of knowing. Exchanges solve this by giving every message a

. A subscriber's software tracks the last number it received, and if the next message jumps from, say, 40,001 straight to 40,003, it knows immediately that message 40,002 never arrived, and it must either request a retransmission or fall back to a fresh snapshot to resynchronize its view of the book.

body.text: Everything Chapter 3 covered, kernel bypass, FPGAs, nanosecond-level hardware logic, is wasted if the feed parser sitting in front of it cannot detect a dropped packet. A strategy trading on a silently incomplete view of the order book is not fast, it is wrong. Gap detection has to run inline, as part of the same latency-critical path as everything else, not as a slower background check.

body.title: Why multicast at all
body.question: Why do exchanges use multicast for market data instead of a dedicated connection per subscriber, given that multicast cannot guarantee delivery?
options: Multicast is cheaper for the exchange to license
Multicast lets one broadcast reach unlimited subscribers at once, which scales far better than one connection per client, and the sequence number system handles the delivery risk
Dedicated connections are not technically possible for real-time data
Multicast automatically retransmits any dropped packet, so there is no real downside
body.explanation: Multicast scales because a single broadcast reaches every listening subscriber, avoiding the cost of managing a separate connection for each one. The tradeoff is that it cannot guarantee delivery, which is exactly why sequence numbers exist: to let each subscriber detect and recover from a dropped packet on its own.

body.label: Regulatory Shift
body.context: As covered in the previous chapter, SEBI's post-2015 reforms pushed exchanges toward making tick-by-tick data available to trading members generally, not just those paying for a colocated feed, narrowing one source of information asymmetry.

body.text: A market data feed is not one product. It is a tradeoff between how much detail you need and how much infrastructure you are willing to build to survive that detail arriving imperfectly.

points: Snapshot feeds broadcast periodic order book state, while tick-by-tick (TBT) feeds announce every individual event in the exact sequence the matching engine processed it.
Exchanges distribute market data over multicast so a single broadcast can reach any number of subscribers, rather than managing one connection per client.

Multicast does not guarantee delivery, so every message carries a sequence number, letting a subscriber detect a dropped packet and recover by requesting a retransmission or falling back to a snapshot.
Gap detection has to run as part of the same latency-critical path as the rest of a trading system's feed handling. A fast strategy trading on an incomplete book is not an edge, it is a bug.
